DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026 (The Copper Kettle)

**What the paper proposes.** Raise the prices of fish and chips, the burger and the steak, and replace the mushroom risotto with a seasonal vegetarian special. The paper projects £42,000 a year of extra gross profit and a main-course margin of about 71%.

The groundwork is solid, and most of the figures check out:
- **Table 1 margins:** all five are correct (69%, 72%, 75%, 60% and 80%).
- **Plates:** the weekly total adds to 1,050.
- **Competitor prices:** all three new prices sit below the midpoint of the competitor range (£17.98, £16.50 and £29.50).
- **Weekly gain:** £810 × 52 = £42,120 is right on the paper's own assumptions.

But the risotto decision is based on a misreading of Table 1, and the projection ignores the beef price rise that section 4 itself reports. After correcting both, the price rises roughly offset rising costs rather than restoring margin.

## 1. The risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu

Section 5.2 says the risotto has "the weakest margin on the menu." Table 1 shows **80%, the highest of any dish**:
- **Per plate:** it makes £11.20, more than the burger (£10.80) or the curry (£10.90).
- **Sales:** its 90 plates a week are the lowest, but tied with specials.

Replacing it with a special could *reduce* profit. Specials run at a 64% margin. At the same £14 price and that margin, the 90 plates would make about **£200 a week less**.

Two other considerations:
- **It may be the only vegetarian main.** Vegetarian diners often decide where a group eats, so removal could cost more than the risotto's own sales.
- **There's a stronger option.** Keep the risotto, or replace it only with a special costed to match its margin.

## 2. The projection ignores the beef price rise

Section 4 reports beef prices **rising 12% from 1 April**, the same day the new prices start. The projection doesn't account for this.

| | Burger | Steak |
|---|---|---|
| Food cost now | £4.20 | £10.40 |
| +12% (upper bound) | +£0.50 | +£1.25 |
| Weekly extra cost | ~£131 | ~£150 |

That is up to **£281 a week**. It's an upper bound, because the rise applies to the beef in each dish, not to the chips or the bun. Even so, most of the burger's £1 increase and much of the steak's £2 are needed just to cover beef.

**Effect on margin:**
- **Current main-course margin:** about 69–70%, depending on the price of specials (Table 1 doesn't give it).
- **Price rises alone:** about 71%, which matches the paper.
- **Including the beef rise:** about **69–70%, roughly unchanged.** The increases cover rising costs; they don't restore margin.

## 3. VAT may overstate the gain

UK menu prices must include VAT. At your turnover (roughly £850,000 a year on main courses alone), you are well above the VAT threshold. If Table 1's prices include VAT:
- **£810 of extra menu revenue** is about £675 to the business.
- **Margin percentages** are also overstated on a net-of-VAT basis.

Check how your accountant calculates margin.

## 4. Revised projection (illustrative)

| | Weekly | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| Paper's figure | £810 | £42,120 |
| Less beef rise (upper bound) | £529 | ~£27,500 |
| Net of VAT, less beef | ~£394 | ~£20,500 |
| Also replacing risotto with a 64%-margin special | ~£190 | ~£10,000 |

The real gain is probably **£10,000–£27,000 a year**, not £42,000. That still justifies the price rises, especially to absorb beef costs, but on different grounds than the paper gives.

## 5. "Volumes will hold" needs testing

- **Repeat customers are not necessarily insensitive to price.** Regulars are the guests most likely to *notice* increases.
- **The 2024 increase** "had no visible effect on bookings." But bookings aren't plates per dish, and guests may switch to cheaper dishes.
- **Add a break-even test.** For example, fish and chips can lose about 8% of volume (11.40 ÷ 12.40) before the increase loses money. A break-even figure for each dish would give the owners a clear trigger.

## 6. Monitoring will be misled by the season

Comparing April–May against a January–February baseline mixes the price effect with seasonal change, since spring trade naturally differs from winter. Compare with April–May 2025, or track each dish's *share* of mains rather than absolute plates.

## 7. Smaller points

- **Trading days.** The recommendation says "six trading days a week," but section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five. The weekly figures are unaffected; fix the text.
- **Lunch.** It's described as "a small share" of main courses, but no figure is given. Check the till data, since lunch is where price sensitivity is highest.

## How the cover note differs from the document

| Cover note | The data |
|---|---|
| Risotto has "the weakest margin" | The highest, at 80% |
| £42,000 a year | ~£10,000–27,000 after beef, VAT and the risotto |
| Margin lifts to ~71% | Roughly unchanged once beef costs rise |
| A loyal base means volumes hold | Asserted, not tested |

## What to fix before the owners decide

1. Keep the risotto, or replace it only with a special at a similar margin.
2. Include the beef cost increase in the projection and the margin figure.
3. Confirm whether prices and margins include VAT.
4. Add break-even volumes per dish, and monitor against the same weeks last year.
5. Fix the trading-days error.

The price increases are sensible, since prices stay competitive and beef costs are rising. But the paper should present them as protecting margin rather than restoring it. The risotto decision should be reversed.
